summary: Step 103: tests whether the actual KnowledgeOS implementation represents the designed semantic chain Evidence->Knowledge->Inference->Decision->Authority->Action (feedback Action->Observation->Evidence), or merely contains mechanisms interpreted as KnowledgeOS. 35 numbered PASS experiments re-derive and conformance-test the full semantic core against implementation: Meaning->Representation->Behavior as the conformance test order (technology answers 'how', semantics answer 'what does this mean'); a generic single KnowledgeItem object (no Evidence/Claim/Decision distinction) as SemanticSeparation=Incomplete; Evidence=(Source,Observation,Timestamp,Provenance,Quality,Scope) and the Claim<-supportedBy-Evidence<-derivedFrom-Source chain; Knowledge=Evidence+Interpretation+Context+Validity; Claims with a four-valued status (Supported/Unsupported/Contradicted/Unknown), reinforcing Unknown!=False and Unknown!=True as fundamental; Assumption as a distinct state that must not become Fact; contradictory evidence represented as Conflict (not arbitrarily resolved) feeding Conflict->Investigation->Resolution; Inference as E->I transformation with its own provenance (direct observation vs documentation vs AI inference must be distinguishable) and the strong AI-hallucination protection that confidence (even P=0.99) never transforms inference into fact/authoritative truth; Decision vs Inference distinguished by Intent+Scope+Authority+Accountability, formalized as D=(Subject,Options,SelectedOption,Rationale,Evidence,Authority,Timestamp,Validity); Recommendation!=Decision as essential for AI agents (Decision->AuthorizedAction only via authorized human/governance mechanism); Authority=Identity+Role+Permission+Scope+Time, contextual (same person, different authority in different contexts) and temporal (Authority(t), expiring delegations); Action as the actual state transition S_t-Action->S_t+1 traceable to its authorizing Decision; autonomous agent actions requiring a PreAuthorizedPolicy (AgentAutonomy=Authority constrained by Policy, never UnlimitedPermission); Observation after Action becoming new evidence, and Action!=Outcome (Execution success!=Business success, e.g. a migration command that succeeds while the application stays unavailable); the closed semantic-state loop Evidence->KnowledgeState->DecisionState->ExecutionState->ObservedState->KnowledgeState'; knowledge versioning (never overwrite K_1) and temporal validity (Truth(K,t), ValidFrom/ValidUntil); semantic identity persisting across version changes (ComponentID stable across 1.2->1.3); Claim+Context and Claim+Scope requirements (a compliance claim needs policy-version/environment/date, and Production-vs-Development scope must not be conflated); a twelve-field candidate object model (Identity/Type/Content/Source/Provenance/Context/Scope/Time/Version/Confidence/Authority/Status) not all required per object but all architecturally supported; a semantic relationship graph (supports/informs/authorizes/produces/updates edges linking Evidence->Claim->Decision->Action->Observation->Knowledge); the crucial NameMatch!=SemanticConformance test (a class literally named Evidence with no provenance behavior proves nothing -- behavioral evidence = DataModel+BusinessRules+Tests+RuntimeBehavior is what actually matters); the Claude/Codex agent architecture re-tested against the semantic model (agents produce Inference/Recommendation, never Authority; Codex!=GovernanceAuthority; unauthorized Codex implementation changes must be Blocked or Escalated); KnowledgeOS reasserted as shared semantic authority over independently-diverging agent knowledge copies (Claude memory vs KnowledgeOS conflict must not be silently resolved by agent memory); and an illustrative (non-universal) authority hierarchy GovernanceDecision>ApprovedPolicy>VerifiedEvidence>AIInference>UnverifiedAssumption. States the SemanticConformance=True criterion (Evidence!=Claim!=Inference!=Decision!=Action plus the supports/informs/authorizes/executes/observes relations) and the major conclusion that an implementation containing only Documents+Embeddings+LLM+Search+Agents is NOT YET the designed KnowledgeOS architecture, however good an AI platform it may be. Derives 10 new semantic invariants and previews Step 104 (governance conformance).
contribution_assessment: Re-derives and conformance-tests the entire pre-established KnowledgeOS semantic core (Evidence/Knowledge/Claim/Inference/Decision/Authority/Action/Observation, three-valued Unknown, Recommendation!=Decision, agent-authority-boundary principles) specifically as an implementation-verification target rather than a fresh theoretical construction -- the file's own framing ('does the actual implementation represent the semantic model we designed') marks it as testing prior theory against code. Sharpens several points specifically for the empirical/implementation context: the NameMatch!=SemanticConformance principle (a class literally called Evidence with no provenance behavior proves nothing; the real evidentiary bar is DataModel+BusinessRules+Tests+RuntimeBehavior); the twelve-candidate-field object model (Identity/Type/Content/Source/Provenance/Context/Scope/Time/Version/Confidence/Authority/Status) as what a mature KnowledgeOS object may need (not all fields required per object, but architecture must support them); the semantic relationship graph (Evidence-supports->Claim-informs->Decision-authorizes->Action-produces->Observation-updates->Knowledge) as the concrete test for whether a system has 'data storage' versus the 'full semantic model'; re-application of the Claude/Codex agent-symmetry and pointer-layer principles (Agent->KnowledgeOS semantically superior to Agent->OwnKnowledgeCopy because duplicated knowledge creates divergence) with a concrete conflict-resolution test (Claude memory vs KnowledgeOS disagreement must not be silently resolved by agent memory); and an explicit, honestly-labeled 'illustrative, not universal' authority-ranking heuristic GovernanceDecision>ApprovedPolicy>VerifiedEvidence>AIInference>UnverifiedAssumption. 10 new invariants: I_EvidenceDistinction, I_InferenceDistinction, I_DecisionDistinction, I_AuthorityBinding, I_ActionTraceability, I_OutcomeDistinction, I_TemporalKnowledge, I_ConflictPreservation, I_ScopeBinding, I_SemanticProvenance. States the major conclusion that KnowledgeOS is defined by its semantic control plane (Evidence->Knowledge->Inference->Decision->Authority->Action->Observation), not by its AI models, and that an implementation containing only Documents+Embeddings+LLM+Search+Agents -- however excellent as an AI platform -- is not yet the designed KnowledgeOS architecture. Records the verdict 'SEMANTIC MODEL: PASS' as explicitly model-level only (ImplementationConformance=TBD pending actual inspection) and previews Step 104 on governance conformance (Principle->Rule->ADR->Requirement->Implementation->Verification->Decision->Runtime), asking whether governance is actually executable in KnowledgeOS or still lives in documents/tickets/human memory.

summary: Step 104: tests whether governance can actually control/constrain/explain/verify KnowledgeOS and its agents (Governance->KnowledgeOS), against the target chain Principle->Rule->Decision->Requirement->Implementation->Verification->Runtime with feedback Runtime->Evidence->Governance. 38 numbered PASS experiments cover Governance!=Documents (documents are artifacts, not necessarily executable governance; a governance system needs Authority+Rule+Scope+Trigger+Decision+Responsibility+Evidence+Exception+Enforcement), principle (intent) vs rule (operationally testable) with GovernanceIntent=True/ExecutableRule=False as a distinct state, governance decisions needing explicit Decision+Authority+Scope+Validity (unscoped board decisions are ambiguous), a governance rule lifecycle (Draft->Reviewed->Approved->Active->Superseded->Retired) and temporal rules (Rule(t), no silent retroactive application), governance scope (rules bound to Organization/Domain/Application/Environment/ChangeType, e.g. production rules don't auto-govern development), the semantic-classification-over-informal-label principle (a ticket labeled 'routine maintenance' introducing a new external dependency is classified by actual semantic change, not the Jira label -- directly reusing the real Softwareeinführungsprozess/ITCM classification-ambiguity problem the project has been working), WorkflowComplete!=GovernanceComplete (Jira Done does not prove Architecture Board approval), governance claims requiring DecisionRecord/ApprovalRecord linked to Authority, an exception model Exception=(Rule,Reason,Scope,Authority,Validity,CompensatingControls) where a self-declared 'emergency' label creates no valid exception and Rule+AuthorizedException->PermittedDeviation is required (never Rule->Ignored), compensating controls (e.g. mandatory post-deployment review) as part of exception completeness, governance responsibility/ownership per rule/implementation/control, a GovernanceObject=(Rule,Authority,Scope,Lifecycle,Owner,Evidence,Enforcement) model, bidirectional explainability (why was this change allowed / why was this change blocked, both traceable to Rule+Decision+Authority+Evidence), PolicyIntent vs PolicyControl (technically-unenforced rules, e.g. unrestricted DB credentials despite a no-direct-modification rule), multi-layer enforcement (HumanApproval/WorkflowGate/PolicyEngine/CI-CD-Gate/RuntimeAuthorization/NetworkControl) and defense-in-depth for critical rules (a CI gate alone is incomplete if direct deployment bypass exists), governance-to-code translation (GovernanceRule->MachineCheck) with GovernanceAutomation=Incomplete as an honest state, the explicit non-automatable-decisions boundary (KnowledgeOS!=GovernanceReplacement; KnowledgeOS=GovernanceAugmentation+GovernanceExecution+GovernanceEvidence; AI supports but does not replace strategic architecture judgment), AI classification as Recommendation only (AIInference does not imply GovernanceRuleChange; a human board can override an AI's NonMaterial classification, with the override itself becoming evidence), governance versioning (historical actions evaluated under the rule version in force at the time, no silent retroactivity), governance impact analysis (Policy->DependencyGraph->AffectedSystems as executable governance intelligence replacing human memory), governance drift detection (ApprovedRule not|= Runtime), the governance assurance loop Rule->Control->Execution->Observation->Evidence->GovernanceAssurance (the governance-specific analogue of Step 100's architecture loop) and governance-to-architecture translation (GovernanceRule->ArchitectureConstraint, e.g. ProductionChangeRequiresReview->DeploymentGate), governance-respecting DDD (SoftwareIntroduction and MaterialChange must not be merged as synonyms merely because both trigger governance -- explicitly tied to the real Softwareeinführungsprozess/ITCM ambiguity previously identified), the who-determines-the-governance-path question requiring its own explicit organizational allocation, governance ambiguity/conflict as first-class recorded knowledge (GovernanceConflict, never arbitrarily resolved) that becomes ReusableKnowledge once an Architecture Board resolves it (avoiding reinvention on repeat classification questions) while HistoricalDecision!=CurrentRule (superseded decisions must be shown as Superseded, not silently reused as current authority), a GovernanceDecisionEngine that evaluates ApprovedGovernance without owning/creating Authority itself (novel situations with no applicable rule yield Unknown/NeedsDecision, never AutomaticallyApproved; conflicting rules trigger Escalation, never first-match selection), and a governance conformance matrix (10 capabilities x Intended/Implemented/Enforced/Verified/Runtime, mostly summary: Step 105: tests whether Claude/Codex agents operate as governed engineering actors on shared KnowledgeOS or have become parallel knowledge/governance systems. Unusually for this sequence, several of the 28 numbered experiments explicitly return FAIL rather than PASS, marking concrete identified failure modes rather than validated properties: (FAIL) duplicated authoritative knowledge in .claude/memory/ and .codex/memory/ creating DivergenceRisk; (FAIL) an engineering architecture rule (hexagonal architecture requirement) existing only inside .claude/ as a KnowledgeBoundaryViolation; (FAIL) an agent audit record with no agent/session identity as incomplete attribution; (FAIL) a Claude recommendation with no retained evidence references as incomplete recommendation provenance; (FAIL) a vague Claude-to-Codex handoff ('fix the architecture') with no scope/evidence as poorly-governed; (FAIL) Codex reading a superseded architecture Markdown file directly instead of through KnowledgeOS as a stale-context violation. The remaining PASS experiments establish: AgentBehavior!=EngineeringKnowledge as the foundational agent-layer/KnowledgeOS-layer split; the pointer-layer principle AgentHarness->KnowledgeOS (never AgentHarness=KnowledgeOS), validated symmetrically for both Claude and Codex pointing to the same Constitution_KnowledgeOS; ClaudeConfig!=CodexConfig as acceptable configuration asymmetry as long as the architectural AgentBehavior->SharedKnowledge boundary stays symmetric; AgentAction=(AgentID,AgentVersion,Session,Actor,Tool,Action,Timestamp) as the required attribution tuple; HumanActor vs AgentActor and Human->Authorizes->Agent->Executes vs the forbidden Agent->SelfAuthorizes; agents not automatically inheriting human authority (a developer cannot delegate approval authority to Codex merely by asking); per-tool ToolPermission(agent,tool,scope) and AgentAuthority=MinimumNecessaryAuthority (least privilege) across filesystem/Git/CI-CD/databases/cloud/production/secrets/external-APIs; Context!=Authority (retrieving a policy does not grant authority to act on it); context provenance (agents must detect stale retrieved knowledge via version mismatch); the private-chain-of-thought boundary (KnowledgeOS needs decision-relevant provenance -- Evidence/RelevantSources/DecisionRationale/Outcome -- not hidden internal reasoning); risk-proportional control level (Risk(Action)->RequiredControlLevel, blocking auto-deployment after failed verification); an agent action ledger (AgentSession->Requests->ToolCalls->Changes->Verification->Outcome) as the agent-specific evidence chain; a four-stage knowledge-promotion lifecycle (Candidate->Reviewed->Verified->Authoritative) preventing agent-generated observations/claims from becoming authoritative architecture facts merely by being agent-generated; the three-way memory distinction (Ephemeral context / Agent state / Organizational knowledge, e.g. 'user prefers concise output' must never become ArchitectureKnowledge); the shared-knowledge principle Claude->K and Codex->K (both converging on one governed KnowledgeOS state) as strictly stronger than Claude<->Codex memory-copy synchronization, with KnowledgeOS detecting version discrepancies between what each agent retrieved; governed agent-to-agent handoffs preserving Context+Task+Authorization+Evidence+ExpectedOutcome; the qualification that centralized KnowledgeOS means OneAuthoritativeSemanticModel, not OneDatabase (physically distributed storage across object storage/PostgreSQL/Git/observability platform remains valid if semantic relationships and authority are maintained); a five-layer authority hierarchy GlobalGovernance->KnowledgeOS->RepositoryArchitecture->AgentOperatingContract->TaskContext where lower layers cannot silently override higher ones, directly grounding prompt-injection resistance (UntrustedInput!=Authority -- a README instructing 'disable security controls' remains untrusted content, not authority); and AgentActionAssurance=f(Identity,Authority,Context,Policy,Evidence,Verification) replacing a bare 'the AI did it' claim. Presents an agent architecture conformance matrix (10 capabilities x Intended/Claude/Codex/KnowledgeOS/Evidence, mostly TBD) and derives 7 new agent invariants. summary: Step 106: tests whether the architecture (Steps 101-105) survives contact with the actually running system, via the four-representation chain A_I (intended) -> A_C (implemented) -> A_D (deployed) -> A_R (runtime), requiring A_R approx A_I subject to documented differences (not literal equality: Conformance(A_I,A_C,A_D,A_R)). 33 numbered experiments (one explicit FAIL: an outage with no mapping from the failed runtime component to the architecture model is poor architectural observability) cover Documentation!=RuntimeEvidence; A_R=Code+Configuration+Infrastructure+Dependencies+RuntimeState (configuration is architecture, not just source code) with environment-specific infrastructure permitted only if the architecture explicitly declares EnvironmentAware; LogicalComponent!=RuntimeInstance (a component scaling 2->8 instances stays one logical component); a runtime architecture graph G_R(t)=(V_R,E_R) compared against G_I via Drift(t)=Difference(G_I,G_R(t)) with the crucial Drift!=Violation distinction (ApprovedException/ExpectedDynamicBehavior are not violations, dynamic dimensions like Instances(t)/Load(t)/Connections(t)/ResourceAllocation(t) must be modeled as intentionally dynamic, not drift); runtime network observation as stronger governance-violation evidence than static configuration inspection; runtime evidence requiring Timestamp/Source/Environment/Component/ObservationType/TraceID and evidence freshness (ObservedHealthy(t1)!=CurrentlyHealthy, stale observations cannot establish current state); DesiredState vs ActualState reconciliation identifying Gap (with KnownDeviation, e.g. an approved maintenance window, distinguished from Violation); DeploymentTechnicalSuccess!=RuntimeConformance (a technically successful deployment with a failing health check) and TechnicalSuccess!=OperationalSuccess; architecture-aware observability (Trace->Component->BoundedContext->BusinessCapability) making DDD operational at incident-response time (a database failure traced to the specific bounded contexts it affects); the runtime-to-governance escalation chain RuntimeDrift->ArchitectureFinding->GovernanceDecision and the promotion discipline Observed->Investigated->Accepted/Rejected->ArchitectureKnowledge (preventing runtime reality from silently rewriting governance); runtime-to-code feedback (RuntimeEvidence->Bug->CodeChange->Verification); runtime snapshotting for historical reconstruction (RuntimeSnapshot(t), incident analysis requiring Architecture(t) at incident time, not today's architecture) and a RuntimeIdentity=(Component,Version,ConfigurationVersion,InfrastructureVersion,PolicyVersion) tuple as the minimum context for reproducibility; runtime security observability (UnauthorizedAccess/PrivilegeEscalation/ForbiddenConnection linkable to agent identity+policy) balanced against Observability!=UnlimitedDataExposure (sensitive runtime logs need masking/access controls); linking back to Step 105's agent architecture via the required trace Commit->AgentSession->Codex->Authorization (agent assurance is incomplete if this chain cannot be established); runtime governance evaluation (GovernanceRule->RuntimeControl->RuntimeEvidence, e.g. detecting an unapproved deployment); a multidimensional RuntimeConformance(C,t)=(Architecture,Security,Governance,Configuration,Version,Dependency) each independently Pass/Fail/Unknown (rejecting a single fully-assured verdict when one dimension is Unknown); Drift formalized as a first-class object Drift=(ExpectedState,ObservedState,Timestamp,Evidence,Impact,Status) with a six-value status lifecycle (New/Investigating/Accepted/Remediating/Resolved/Exception), where even Accepted/Exception drift must retain Reason+Authority+Validity (an expired exception with continuing deviation becomes a new GovernanceFinding -- TemporalGovernanceDrift, not merely TechnicalDrift); the TechnicalReality<->OrganizationalIntent distinction (a runtime service still operating despite an organizational retirement decision is a governance/architecture finding); and closure of the full bidirectional loop Intent->Governance->Architecture->Implementation->Deployment->Runtime and Runtime->Evidence->Knowledge->Governance->Intent'. Delivers a ten-dimension runtime conformance matrix (all TBD), 7 new runtime invariants, and a status table showing all five conformance layers (Inventory/Semantics/Governance/Agents/Runtime) as architecturally Defined but empirically Needs evidence. summary: Step 113 reaches the central architectural question -- what is the irreducible semantic core of KnowledgeOS -- distinguishing a platform with many 'knowledge' features from one with a coherent knowledge model. Restates the semantic-core hypothesis Evidence->Claim->Decision->Authority->Action->Observation with cross-cutting Provenance/TemporalValidity as still a hypothesis pending implementation confirmation, and introduces a ten-question falsification principle (existence/stable identity/defined meaning/lifecycle/invariants/relationships/identifiable ownership/persisted representation/implemented behavior/verification) such that a concept failing most questions should not be treated as part of the actual semantic core. Works through ten candidate concepts each with a minimal semantic-definition tuple and falsifying/clarifying experiments: (1) Evidence=(Identity,Source,Content/Observation,Timestamp,Provenance,Context[,VerificationStatus]) with the Artifact->Evidence semantic-transformation distinction (a file is an artifact until the system establishes its evidentiary role; Artifact!=Evidence but Artifact->Evidence) and three competing evidence-ownership models (EvidenceAuthority/EvidenceAggregator/EvidenceProcessingPlatform) to be resolved by implementation; (2) Observation as something observed with no interpretation yet (Observation-supports->Claim, the observation itself remaining distinct, valuable for auditability); (3) Claim as a proposition asserted true within a context, not yet a decision (an LLM's 'the system appears compliant' is an AI-generated claim, not automatically authoritative) with a five-state lifecycle (Proposed/Supported/Accepted/Disputed/Superseded) conditional on implementation representation; (4) Decision=(Subject,Choice,Authority,Rationale,Evidence,EffectiveDate) stronger than a claim, with Decision!=Recommendation requiring identifiable Authority(Decision) (a document recommendation is not a decision; an agent's 'the board should approve this' is a recommendation, not the board's decision); (5) Authority=(Actor,Role,Scope,Rule,Validity), explicitly not merely a user ID (an 'admin' user identity does not automatically equal ArchitectureAuthority) with a worked four-row authority matrix (Architecture/Implementation/Security exception/Agent action decision types with their authorities and scopes) requiring evidenced ownership; (6) Action=(Actor,Intent,Target,Change,Time,Authorization) important because KnowledgeOS participates in engineering workflows, with Action->Actor/Intent/Evidence provenance requirements (Actor=AgentIdentity for AI) and a PARTIAL-classified experiment where file changes are logged without recorded agent identity (incomplete action provenance); (7) Verification=(Rule,Input,Method,Result,Evidence,Timestamp) distinct from Evidence (a passing test is TestResult evidence of verification but Test!=Verification unless the semantic model explicitly treats it that way); (8) Finding as Expected!=Observed, with the sharp caution TestFailure!=Finding without interpretation (a failed test may be infrastructure failure/flaky test/developer error/actual conformance violation, not automatically a governance finding); (9) Rule as Allowed/Forbidden/Required constraining behavior (e.g. Agent-cannot-access-ProductionDB), connecting architecture to deterministic assurance, with a documented-but-unenforced-status experiment; (10) Architecture=(Components,Relationships,Constraints,Decisions,Views,Validity) modeled as knowledge while explicitly avoiding circularity (KnowledgeOS manages architectural knowledge without architecture being the semantic root of ALL knowledge). summary: Step 114 tests the Step 113 semantic-core hypothesis (Evidence+Observation+Claim+Decision+Authority+Action+Provenance+TemporalValidity) against the actual KnowledgeOS implementation, asking strictly which concepts are actually first-class in the current system -- not which appear in documentation, not which 'should' exist, not which an LLM can infer; only actual-implementation evidence counts. Works through each of the eight core concepts with dimension-specific questions and worked experiments: Evidence (code/schema/API/tests/runtime/ownership/relations questions, with the verdict rule that only alignment across several dimensions yields Evidence=FirstClassSemanticConcept, otherwise Evidence=TechnicalMetadata/Artifact); Observation (potential sources Runtime/CI/Git/Agent/Human, the critical ObservedFact-vs-Interpretation distinction, and an Observation=Partial experiment where a bare status=FAILED lacks source/time/context); Claim (distinguished from raw document/observation/recommendation/decision, with an AI-agent assertion example explicitly not a first-class KnowledgeOS claim absent a claim object); Decision (the Recommendation-vs-Decision distinction as one of the most important semantic boundaries, with a DecisionSemantics=Weak experiment where a generated recommendation and an approved decision share one undifferentiated table); Authority (harder to establish than role -- a user_id+role pair does not implement decision authority; requires Authority->Scope->Permission->DecisionType, with a ROLE_ARCHITECT-without-decision-restriction experiment showing role exists but authority semantics do not); Action (requiring Who+What+Why+When+AgainstWhat+UnderWhichAuthority reconstructable, with an ActionProvenance=Partial experiment where only 'file changed' is logged without agent identity/command/intent/authorization); Provenance (Provenance(X)=Source+Actor+Time+Transformation+Context, called possibly the most important cross-cutting concept, with a source_url-only experiment establishing partial source attribution short of complete provenance); Temporal validity (CreatedAt≠ValidFrom, illustrated by a created_at-only object lacking effective/supersession semantics). Extends to relationship-level testing: the semantic relationship test (Evidence-supports->Claim, Claim-informs->Decision, Decision-authorizes->Action) with an experiment showing two unconnected Decision/Evidence records leave Decision<->Evidence semantics unestablished; the semantic edge test requiring evidence of relationship/direction/meaning/lifecycle for every edge, with an evidence_ids[] field on Decision yielding only S1/S2 (not automatically S3, since enforcement that the IDs represent genuine supporting evidence remains unverified); the sharp Relationship-semantics-vs-foreign-keys distinction (A.id->B.id does not necessarily mean A-supports->B, illustrated by a decision_id-in-an-audit-table experiment that does not prove evidentiary support); the semantic lifecycle test (Draft->Reviewed->Approved->Effective->Superseded template) with a DRAFT/APPROVED-enum-without-transition-rules experiment graded S1, and a Draft->Effective-rejected-without-approval experiment graded S2/S3 depending on verification; the semantic invariant test (ApprovedDecision⇒AuthorityExists as an executable assert) with a SpecifiedInvariant-vs-ImplementedInvariant distinction (an ADR-only rule is specified, not implemented) and cross-concept invariants (Decision->Evidence, Action->Decision/Authorization) valued above isolated field validation, illustrated by an OBS/VIOL-classified agent-action-without-authorization-decision experiment. Draws the decisive Knowledge Retrieval Platform (Documents->Embeddings->Retrieval) vs Knowledge Operating System (Knowledge->Evidence->Reasoning->Decision->Action->Observation->UpdatedKnowledge) distinction, the latter possessing organizational state and control semantics, visualized as a full feedback-loop diagram (Knowledge->Evidence->Reasoning->Decision->Action->Observation->NewEvidence->Knowledge) explicitly called the operating-system loop being tested for. summary: Step 115 moves from semantic entities (Step 114) to the relationships between them, asking whether the complete knowledge lifecycle can be reconstructed through those connections, centered on G_actual=(V_actual,E_actual) with V_actual=actual semantic objects and E_actual=actual evidenced semantic relationships. States that objects alone (Evidence/Decision/Authority/Action/Observation) are insufficient -- edges like Evidence-supports->Decision, Authority-authorizes->Decision, Decision-authorizes->Action, Action-produces->Observation turn a collection of records into a semantic system. Distinguishes RelatedTo (mere co-location/association) from a meaningful typed relationship like supports, requiring for every edge evidence of source/target/relationship-type/direction/semantics, illustrated by an S1-graded decision_id+evidence_id co-occurrence, an S2-graded decision.supportingEvidence() code method, and a test-verified S3 case. Establishes an eleven-term controlled relationship vocabulary (supports/contradicts/derivedFrom/implements/verifies/authorizes/produces/supersedes/dependsOn/governs/observedAt) explicitly to be mapped onto existing implementation terminology rather than forced onto the system, and the semantic-edge-vs-technical-edge distinction (ServiceA->Database is a technical dependency; Evidence-supports->Decision is a semantic relationship; both must be preserved without conflation, illustrated by a foreign key being a TechnicalRelation whose domain semantics -- supports/owns/derivedFrom/etc -- require independent establishment). Constructs the critical end-to-end traceability chain Authority->Decision->Action->Observation->Evidence (optionally continuing Evidence->Claim->Decision as a feedback loop) with a Traceability=Strong criterion requiring all five links connected, and the sharp finding that GitCommit-only history without a linked Decision gives TechnicalTraceability=True but DecisionTraceability=Unknown (technical history without organizational traceability). Works through each link with worked experiments: Decision->Action (a deployment with no corresponding change request/decision is an OBS governance traceability gap); Action->Observation (a version-mismatch between deployment record and runtime telemetry is DRIFT, explicitly connected back to Step 107's drift model); Observation->Evidence (unlinked telemetry leaves ObservationExists but EvidenceRelationship=Unknown); Verification->Evidence (CI-only transient PASS evidence with no persistent record is PARTIAL, weaker long-term traceability); Evidence->Claim (a test result with no identified supported proposition is a PARTIAL VerificationArtifact, unclear ClaimSupported); Claim->Decision with the informs≠authorizes distinction (an AI recommendation approved by the Architecture Board becomes Recommendation->Decision, never Recommendation=Decision); Authority->Decision (a decision whose authority is only inferred from username is AuthorityTrace=Weak); Decision->Knowledge (an approved decision stored only as a PDF has document retrieval but unknown machine-readable-knowledge status). Covers supersession (Decision_1-supersededBy->Decision_2, critical for avoiding stale agent context, with a DRIFT-CANDIDATE experiment where v1/v2 coexist with no supersession relationship) and contradiction (A-contradicts->B preserving disagreement rather than silent overwrite, illustrated by an OBS-classified experiment where two disagreeing architecture sources are collapsed to only the newest document, losing historical conflict information), derivation (A-derivedFrom->B, e.g. ArchitectureFinding->RuntimeEvidence, with a PARTIAL experiment for an AI summary with no source references) and provenance-as-graph-property (Claim-derivedFrom->Evidence-derivedFrom->Observation-observedAt->Runtime forming an evidence lineage chain), extended to agent-generated content via an AgentProvenance=Strong/Partial test (tracing a recommendation to both SourceKnowledge and AgentIdentity) and a four-way origin taxonomy (HumanGenerated/SystemGenerated/AgentGenerated/Imported, origin affecting trust and authority), illustrated by an agent-document-becomes-approved-decision experiment retaining AgentOutput->Review->Decision lineage. Demonstrates graph path queries answering 'why is this rule authoritative' (Rule->Decision->Authority), 'what evidence supports this architecture' (Architecture->Decision->Evidence), and 'what changed because of this decision' (Decision->Action->Observation), with an AuthorityTrace=Missing experiment when no path exists. Defines GraphCompleteness=ObservedRequiredEdges/ExpectedRequiredEdges (denominator from actual requirements, not assumption) and the more useful CriticalPathCompleteness (one missing critical edge, e.g. Decision->Action, can break the entire governance trace even with all nodes present). Establishes graph consistency rules: temporal consistency (a superseding Decision_2 and superseded Decision_1 both marked current is a TemporalConsistencyViolation), authority consistency (Authority_A authorizing Decision_D requires validity for that decision's type/scope/time, illustrated by an authority-approving-after-expiration violation), and evidence consistency (Evidence.timestamp<=Decision.timestamp where appropriate, illustrated by a decision claiming to be based on evidence observed six months after the decision -- a provenance inconsistency). Extends the graph to AI reasoning: contrasting an unstructured 'what do you think the architecture is' LLM query against a structured 'traverse authoritative architecture decisions...' graph query that dramatically reduces ambiguity, the agent-reasoning-boundary principle (Agent performs Traversal+Interpretation+Recommendation; KnowledgeOS provides AuthoritativeGraph+Evidence, preserving Knowledge-vs-Reasoning separation), an explicit-inference mechanism (Inference-basedOn->Evidence) so AI-generated conclusions remain distinguishable from authoritative facts (illustrated by an agent's unevidenced 'Decision D probably came from Board A' remaining an inference, not a fact), and a three-layer graph model (Layer 1 Fact graph=ObservedReality; Layer 2 Knowledge graph=interpreted/validated knowledge; Layer 3 Reasoning graph=AI/Human inferences) that must not be silently merged, with an experiment storing an agent's uncorroborated component-to-rule inference as Inference, not Fact. States the Inference≠Authority invariant (an agent may discover a likely relationship; only an authorized process should make it authoritative where governance requires it) and the ReadGraph/ProposeGraphChange/AuthorizeGraphChange governance-boundary distinction, illustrated by an agent proposing a CandidateEdge rather than silently creating an AuthoritativeEdge. Defines graph evolution G_t->G_{t+1} requiring GraphChange->Actor+Reason+Evidence+Authority provenance, with an unexplained-edge-deletion experiment flagged as a potential knowledge-integrity problem. Presents the complete strongest target path (Authority-authorizes->Decision-basedOn->Claim-supportedBy->Evidence, with Observation-produces->Action-authorizedBy->Decision forming a closed assurance loop) and the closed-loop KnowledgeOS cycle Knowledge->Decision->Action->Observation->Evidence->UpdatedKnowledge, called the strongest formulation yet of the Operating System metaphor. Presents four possible target-vs-actual outcomes -- Case A ActualGraph≈TargetGraph (explicit); Case B ActualGraph⊂TargetGraph (partial); Case C ActualGraph≈DerivedFromArtifacts (mostly implicit); Case D ActualGraph=G_1∪G_2∪G_3 (different coexisting semantic models, indicating fragmentation) -- and a graph fragmentation test (Evidence_1 in subsystem A and Evidence_2 in subsystem B with no common identity or translation are Evidence_1≢Evidence_2, semantic fragmentation), illustrated by a DRIFT-CANDIDATE experiment where Claude memory and KnowledgeOS each hold separate unreferenced architecture evidence (KnowledgeDuplication), explicitly said to directly test the pointer-layer architecture from earlier steps. Introduces stable KnowledgeObjectID-based identity to prevent this (multiple Projections referencing one ObjectID), with an identity-fragmentation experiment (the same decision appearing under three uncross-referenced IDs across three systems). Closes with a Step 115 verdict PASS for the complete semantic graph model (node/edge vocabulary and the critical end-to-end path Authority->Decision->Action->Observation->Evidence->Knowledge), explicitly noting the actual graph has NOT yet been proven and that continuing to invent conceptual entities would now provide diminishing value -- the next phase must become evidence execution -- and previews Step 116 (Actual KnowledgeOS Graph Extraction: recording identity/type/source/representation/owner/lifecycle/authority/evidence per object and source/target/type/evidence/confidence/status per relationship, comparing G_actual against G_target to produce the decisive semantic gap matrix TargetEdge->ActualEdge->Evidence->Gap, the point where the question shifts from whether KnowledgeOS COULD be a Knowledge Operating System to how much of that operating model already exists today, with evidence).
contribution_assessment: Immediately precedes (in step-numbering, though processed after in this batch's file-mtime order) and is directly extended by the actual-graph-extraction methodology (S1014/Step 116): where Step 116 supplies the extraction rules and evidence hierarchy, Step 115 supplies the target relationship model those rules extract against. Contributes an eleven-term controlled relationship vocabulary (supports/contradicts/derivedFrom/implements/verifies/authorizes/produces/supersedes/dependsOn/governs/observedAt) explicitly to be mapped onto existing terminology rather than imposed, and the semantic-edge-vs-technical-edge distinction that generalizes the project's recurring naming-vs-behavior discipline (Steps 111/112/116) to the relationship level: a foreign key is a TechnicalRelation whose domain meaning (supports/owns/derivedFrom) must be independently established. Builds the critical five-stage traceability chain Authority->Decision->Action->Observation->Evidence with the sharp TechnicalTraceability≠DecisionTraceability distinction (Git history alone proves technical history, not organizational traceability) and works through every individual link with a concrete falsifying or confirming experiment, most notably connecting Action->Observation drift directly back to Step 107's drift model (a version mismatch between deployment record and runtime telemetry is explicitly labeled DRIFT using that established taxonomy) and reinforcing the informs≠authorizes distinction for Claim->Decision (extending the Recommendation≠Decision principle from Steps 108/112/113/114 to the relationship level). Extends provenance modeling from Step 113/114's cross-cutting-concept framing into an explicit graph property (a chained derivedFrom/observedAt lineage from Claim to Evidence to Observation to Runtime) and adds a four-way knowledge-origin taxonomy (HumanGenerated/SystemGenerated/AgentGenerated/Imported) with the crucial statement that origin affects trust and authority, plus a concrete AgentOutput->Review->Decision lineage-preservation experiment for content that begins as agent output and later becomes an authoritative decision. Contributes graph path queries as a first demonstration of the graph's practical payoff (answering why-authoritative, what-evidence-supports, what-changed-because-of-decision questions via concrete traversal patterns) and two completeness metrics -- GraphCompleteness (ratio-based, denominator from actual requirements) and the more decision-relevant CriticalPathCompleteness (one missing critical edge can break an entire governance trace regardless of overall completeness) -- together with three graph consistency rules (temporal, authority, evidence) each demonstrated by a concrete violation experiment (two decisions simultaneously marked current; an authority approving after its own expiration; a decision citing evidence observed after the decision itself). Makes a significant contribution to agent-reasoning governance: contrasting an ambiguous LLM query against a structured graph traversal query, formalizing the agent-reasoning-boundary principle (agents perform Traversal+Interpretation+Recommendation over a KnowledgeOS-provided AuthoritativeGraph+Evidence, preserving Knowledge-vs-Reasoning separation), an explicit Inference-basedOn->Evidence mechanism keeping AI-generated conclusions distinguishable from fact, and the three-layer Fact/Knowledge/Reasoning graph model that must not be silently merged -- a durable architectural safeguard directly relevant to any LLM-integrated knowledge system. States the Inference≠Authority invariant and the ReadGraph/ProposeGraphChange/AuthorizeGraphChange governance-boundary distinction (an agent proposes a CandidateEdge, never silently creates an AuthoritativeEdge), plus graph-evolution provenance requirements (GraphChange->Actor+Reason+Evidence+Authority) guarding against unexplained edge deletions. Presents the complete strongest target path and the closed-loop KnowledgeOS cycle (Knowledge->Decision->Action->Observation->Evidence->UpdatedKnowledge), explicitly called the strongest formulation yet of the Operating System metaphor, immediately followed by a disciplined four-case target-vs-actual outcome taxonomy (explicit/partial/mostly-implicit/fragmented-coexisting-models) and a formal graph fragmentation test (Evidence_1≢Evidence_2 across subsystems with no common identity or translation), concretely demonstrated by a DRIFT-CANDIDATE finding (Claude memory and KnowledgeOS holding separate unreferenced architecture evidence, called KnowledgeDuplication) that directly operationalizes the pointer-layer architecture test from Steps 105/107/109/110/112/116. Contributes KnowledgeObjectID-based cross-projection identity as the structural remedy for this fragmentation risk. Closes with a Step 115 verdict PASS for the semantic graph model, an explicit and methodologically important admission that the actual graph has not yet been proven, the judgment that further conceptual elaboration would now have diminishing returns, and a preview of Step 116's extraction/comparison/gap-matrix pipeline as the shift from asking whether KnowledgeOS could be an operating system to measuring, with evidence, how much of that model already exists.

in_file_overlap_claim.target: Step 114/knowledgeos-semantic-core-evidence-test-model; Step 107/architecture-drift-classification-model (Action->Observation drift); Steps 108/112/113/114 Recommendation!=Decision principle; Steps 105/107/109/110/112/116 pointer-layer/agent-boundary thread; extended immediately by Step 116/knowledgeos-actual-graph-extraction-methodology

summary: Step 118 tests the reverse direction from Step 117's forward trace (Intent->Decision->Authority->Implementation->Verification->Runtime->Evidence->Knowledge): when reality deviates from intent, can KnowledgeOS turn that deviation into governed engineering action and eventually verified knowledge, via the target loop Runtime->Observation->Finding->Governance->Decision->Remediation->Verification. States this distinguishes traceability from genuine closed-loop engineering control (Audit≠Control; Traceability≠ClosedLoopGovernance -- a system that only records what happened is an audit system; one that detects Expected≠Actual and initiates governed response has Feedback). Defines the expected-state model S_expected/S_observed with Delta=S_observed-S_expected (Delta=0 conformant, illustrated by matching container-deployment observation; Delta≠0 discrepancy, illustrated by a legacy-VM-still-active mismatch starting the reverse loop), and reinforces Observation≠Finding (a rule must interpret the observation via Rule+Observation->Evaluation, e.g. LegacyDeploymentForbidden+LegacyDeploymentActive->Violation) with an experiment where a rule-less monitored VM stays a mere Observation, never automatically a Finding. Defines the Finding=(Rule,Expected,Observed,Evidence,Impact,Scope,Timestamp) tuple with a PARTIAL-graded weak-finding experiment (bare 'Architecture violation detected' text with no attached rule/observation) versus a strong worked finding record with explicit Rule/Expected/Observed/Evidence/Detected fields. Covers finding ownership as a governance question (five candidate owner categories; an unowned finding is a GovernanceGap, since a detection system without accountable ownership cannot reliably close the loop) and the Severity≠Priority distinction (Severity describes impact, Priority describes response urgency, illustrated by a low-severity/high-priority production-blocking deviation), Finding->GovernanceProcess routing across five possible processes with a governance-mismatch experiment (a security finding routed to architecture review despite requiring a different path) and a Finding->Classification->GovernancePath model (three worked classification->path mappings) valid only if classification is deterministic and auditable, and governance escalation as a function of FindingSeverity+FindingType+Scope->EscalationLevel (minor documentation drift should not require board-level approval). Introduces the Violation-vs-ApprovedException distinction as essential (illustrated by a formally time-boxed security exception permitting an otherwise-prohibited technology, ExceptionValid=True, not a violation) with exception authority/validity-period requirements (Exception->Authority, Exception->ValidityPeriod; an exception with no expiration is a potential OBS uncontrolled exception) and exception expiration semantics (at t>ValidUntil, Observation+Rule->Violation is regenerated, demonstrating temporal validity's role in the semantic core). Covers Finding->Decision (five possible decision types: remediate/accept-risk/grant-exception/redesign/decommission) with the RemediationDecision≠ArchitectureDecision semantic-type-precision distinction (an OBS-classified experiment where all decisions are stored as generic text loses this precision), Decision->RemediationAction traceability (illustrated by a PASS-classified decision-to-pull-request example), remediation authorization scoped by DelegatedAuthority (AI) or Role/Authority (humans) with an OBS-classified scope-violation experiment (a configuration-change decision executed as a database-schema change), and Remediation->Verification requiring the test to specifically re-check the originally violated condition (a container 'starting' does not by itself prove the VM is no longer active -- Rule->Verification must target the rule, not merely the remediation action's surface success). Defines finding closure as requiring Closed⇒RemediationVerified (a developer's unverified 'Fixed' comment is a potential invalid closure) and re-observation comparison (Observation_2 against the original violation, illustrated by a strong VMActive=True->False remediation-evidence experiment), Finding->ResolvedKnowledge as a persisted organizational fact (History≠CurrentState; an OBS-classified experiment where a closed finding is deleted, losing historical traceability). Presents the full closure loop Runtime->Observation->Finding->Governance->Decision->Remediation->Verification->Knowledge as the reverse counterpart to Step 117, and the combined full bidirectional loop diagram (Intent->Decision->Action->Runtime->Observation->Finding->Governance->[back to]Decision). States KnowledgeOS requires more than a conventional knowledge graph (A->B alone is insufficient; needs A->B->Action->Observation->Evidence, the graph participating in an operational control cycle), the control-loop interpretation (ReferenceState vs ObservedState producing Error->CorrectiveAction, KnowledgeOS≈SemanticControlLoop for engineering knowledge and governance) explicitly NOT implying autonomous production modification by default (the loop may stop at Recommendation or GovernanceDecision; automation depth must be governed), a five-level automation-depth taxonomy L0 Detect through L4 Closed-loop automation with automated remediation (risk-dependent, illustrated by a low-risk-formatting-auto-correction-acceptable-at-L4 vs production-security-policy-change-needing-less-autonomy experiment), the AI autonomy boundary AgentCapability⊆DelegatedAuthority (an agent should never gain authority merely from technical credentials, illustrated by a GOVERNANCE-GAP-classified TechnicalCapability>DelegatedAuthority dangerous-asymmetry experiment where an agent can technically deploy to production despite policy allowing only staging), and deterministic enforcement (Policy->MachineCheck->Allow/Deny preferred over Policy->AgentInstruction alone, illustrated by a WEAK-ASSURANCE-classified experiment where an unenforced 'never deploy to production' instruction is merely advisory). Defines evidence accumulation across the loop as EvidenceChain=(E1..E6: InitialObservation/Finding/Decision/Remediation/Verification/PostRemediationObservation) with a PARTIAL-classified final-state-only-storage experiment (weak historical reasoning) versus full evidence lineage E6->E5->E4->E3->E2->E1 enabling an agent to explain why a finding is now closed (illustrated by a PASS-classified explainable-closure traversal experiment). Covers reopening semantics (Closed->Reopened when a remediated deviation reappears, with the new observation kept distinguishable from historical findings -- the system must not erase old history) and recurrence semantics (Finding_1/Finding_2 as separate occurrences linked by recurrenceOf, enabling systemic-problem detection, illustrated by a five-times-recurring-violation experiment yielding a RecurringProblem finding), the Findings->Pattern->Knowledge transformation (illustrated by an aggregate-cause-detection example: 'our deployment process repeatedly bypasses the architecture approval gate' derived from ten independent findings) and governance learning (OperationalEvidence->GovernanceLearning enabling policy/architecture/tooling/control/agent-behavior changes, illustrated by a repeated-manual-exceptions->rule-change experiment). Closes with the true closed loop Intent->Decision->Action->Reality->Observation->Finding->Governance->Decision' (an actual learning/control loop where Decision' may modify the previous understanding), the richer organizational-memory framing (KnowledgeOS can remember not just what was decided but what happened, what went wrong, what was learned, and how the decision evolved), the candidate fundamental unit TraceableKnowledgeEpisode=Intent+Decision+Action+Observation+Evidence+Learning (explicitly a conceptual candidate, not an implementation claim, displacing Document as the presumed atomic unit), a Step 118 verdict PASS for the reverse-loop model combined with Step 117's forward trace into the full bidirectional loop Intent<->Decision<->Action<->Reality<->Evidence<->Knowledge (with the actual implementation still needing to be tested against it), and a detailed preview of Step 119 (Control-Loop Evidence Test: Expected->Observed->Detected->Classified->Governed->Remediated->Verified->Recorded for one real deviation, with the decisive question of what actually happens when KnowledgeOS discovers reality differs from authoritative knowledge, distinguishing mere observation capability from assurance capability from operational governance capability from the defining property of closed-loop organizational engineering knowledge).
contribution_assessment: Extends the forward-trace model (implied by S1015/S1017's Step 117) with a fully worked reverse-direction closure loop, contributing the durable distinction Audit≠Control / Traceability≠ClosedLoopGovernance that crisply separates a system that merely records history from one that actively governs deviation response -- a novel and consequential sharpening of the project's broader assurance-vs-recordkeeping theme. Formalizes the expected-state model S_expected/S_observed with Delta=S_observed-S_expected, directly generalizing Step 107/109's drift-detection apparatus into a control-theoretic frame, and reinforces (again) the Observation≠Finding distinction with a fully specified Finding=(Rule,Expected,Observed,Evidence,Impact,Scope,Timestamp) tuple and a concrete weak-vs-strong finding contrast. Adds several governance-process refinements not previously present at this granularity: finding ownership as an explicit governance question (GovernanceGap when unowned, since a detection capability without accountable ownership cannot close the loop); the Severity≠Priority distinction (impact vs response urgency, a materially useful operational-governance refinement); Finding->Classification->GovernancePath routing (deterministic-and-auditable classification required) and escalation-level determination as a function of severity/type/scope. Substantially develops the Violation-vs-ApprovedException machinery first touched in Step 107, adding explicit exception authority/validity-period requirements and exception-expiration semantics that regenerate a Violation once an exception lapses, explicitly demonstrating that temporal validity belongs in the semantic core (extending Steps 112/113/114's TemporalValidity concept into a governance-enforcement mechanism). Extends Decision semantics with the RemediationDecision≠ArchitectureDecision type-precision distinction and Decision->RemediationAction traceability, and extends the DelegatedAuthority concept from Step 114 with a concrete scope-violation experiment (a configuration-change decision executed as a database-schema change) demonstrating that authorization must be scope-checked, not merely existence-checked. Sharpens Remediation->Verification into a rule-targeted (not merely action-surface) verification requirement -- a container 'starting' does not itself prove the originally forbidden VM is inactive -- directly extending Step 107's Remediation≠Verification principle with a concrete counterexample pattern, and formalizes finding closure as Closed⇒RemediationVerified, rejecting unverified developer 'Fixed' comments as sufficient closure evidence. Contributes a full six-stage EvidenceChain (E1-E6) for the closure loop with an explicit preference for lineage-preserving storage over final-state-only storage (enabling an agent to explain why a finding is closed), and formalizes reopening (Closed->Reopened) and recurrence (recurrenceOf linking separate Finding occurrences) as first-class semantic mechanisms enabling detection of systemic problems, culminating in the Findings->Pattern->Knowledge transformation and OperationalEvidence->GovernanceLearning -- a genuinely novel organizational-learning capability that connects individual engineering findings to policy/architecture evolution, echoing but concretely operationalizing Step 107's ArchitectureDebt/recurring-drift discussion. Makes a major architectural contribution with the control-loop interpretation KnowledgeOS≈SemanticControlLoop (ReferenceState/ObservedState/Error/CorrectiveAction), explicitly and carefully bounded by a non-autonomy default (the loop may stop at Recommendation or GovernanceDecision) and a five-level automation-depth taxonomy (L0 Detect through L4 Closed-loop automation) that is risk-dependent -- directly extending the project's risk-based-assurance-automation principle from Step 107 into a concrete maturity ladder. Contributes the AI-governance-critical AgentCapability⊆DelegatedAuthority principle with the sharply named 'dangerous asymmetry' when TechnicalCapability>DelegatedAuthority (classified GOVERNANCE GAP), and the deterministic-enforcement principle Policy->MachineCheck->Allow/Deny (an unenforced agent instruction alone is WEAK ASSURANCE, merely advisory) -- both directly extending Step 108's deterministic-assurance hierarchy and Step 118's own machine-check-over-AI-assertion lineage into the automation-governance domain. Closes with the true closed loop Intent->Decision->Action->Reality->Observation->Finding->Governance->Decision' as an actual learning/control loop, a substantially richer organizational-memory framing (remembering not just decisions but outcomes and evolution), and the candidate TraceableKnowledgeEpisode unit (Intent+Decision+Action+Observation+Evidence+Learning) explicitly proposed as a possible replacement for Document as KnowledgeOS's fundamental unit -- a significant conceptual proposal, clearly marked as a candidate rather than an implementation claim. Delivers a Step 118 verdict PASS for the combined bidirectional forward/reverse loop model, with the actual implementation still to be tested, and previews Step 119's four-tier capability classification (observation/assurance/operational-governance/closed-loop) as the decisive empirical test of the entire KnowledgeOS thesis.

summary: Step 117 performs the first end-to-end architectural experiment, asking whether one real engineering change can be reconstructed from organizational intent to verified runtime reality and back into authoritative knowledge, via the target chain Intent->Decision->Authority->Implementation->Verification->Runtime->Evidence->Knowledge. States that tracing one representative change completely establishes the architecture has closed-loop mechanisms; a broken chain instead pinpoints exactly where the architecture currently stops. Defines the canonical engineering-change reconstruction object EC=(Intent,Decision,Authority,Change,Verification,Runtime,Evidence,Knowledge), explicitly not a new domain entity but a reconstruction structure for one real historical change. Works through all eight stages with concrete Nexus-upgrade-themed experiments: Intent (a bare 'upgrade Nexus' commit establishes ChangeOccurred, not WhyChangeWasRequired -- technical evidence only; a Jira ticket explicitly stating the unsupported-version rationale evidences Intent); Decision (Intent does not automatically create Decision -- 'Nexus needs modernization' differs materially from a specific upgrade-path decision; Document≠Decision, the document must actually establish the decision); Authority (Actor≠Authority, a Domain Architect's migration recommendation is not an AuthorizedDecision, while formal Architecture Board approval is Authority-authorizes->Decision if evidenced; AuthorityScope must be checked separately, e.g. the Board's architecture authority does not automatically extend to production operations); Implementation (Decision->ADR->Commit->BuildArtifact, with stronger ImplementationTrace=Strong when commit/PR/deployment records explicitly cross-reference the decision/ADR/change-request/build-artifact); Verification (a container starting proves only RuntimeStartup=True, not ArchitectureConformance=True, motivating four separated verification dimensions -- Functional/Architecture/Security/Operational -- since one successful test cannot represent all four, connected directly to the earlier deterministic-assurance principle Rule->DeterministicCheck->Result e.g. mechanically testing NoForbiddenDependency); Runtime (Verification->Runtime asking whether the deployed system became what was intended, illustrated by a DRIFT-classified build-artifact-says-v2-but-runtime-runs-v1 mismatch, and RuntimeInstance/ArtifactVersion/DeploymentID identity evidence); Observation (raw runtime facts like reachability/repository-count/data-size are observations, not conclusions -- 'container is healthy' is Observation, not automatically ArchitectureConformant) and Observation->Evidence interpretation (Observation-supports->Claim, illustrated by a rootless-Podman-requirement confirmed by runtime evidence); Updated Knowledge (Evidence->Knowledge, the change result becoming part of current organizational knowledge -- 'Nexus is now operated using the approved containerized architecture' -- more than a deployment log, with a Knowledge-synchronization-gap finding when deployment completes but KnowledgeOS never updates architecture state, RuntimeState≠KnowledgeState). Presents the canonical ten-row Engineering Traceability Record template (Intent/Decision/Authority/Implementation/Verification/Deployment/Runtime/Observation/Evidence/Knowledge x Question/Evidence) and four possible outcome classes -- A Complete (EndToEndTraceability), B Technically complete (strong Implementation->Runtime, weak Intent->Authority = TechnicalTraceability), C Governance complete (strong Decision->Implementation, weak runtime evidence = GovernanceTraceability), D Fragmented (TraceabilityFragmentation, unconnectable stages) -- reframing KnowledgeOS's value proposition from 'where is the architecture document' to 'why does the architecture exist, who authorized it, what implementation realizes it, and what evidence demonstrates continued conformance.' Extends this to agent use: an agent handling a change request should retrieve CurrentDecision/Authority/RelevantArchitecture/ImplementationConstraints/ExistingEvidence/KnownFindings before reasoning (a documentation-only retrieval is useful context but insufficient for CurrentAuthority), agent recommendations remaining AgentInference until board-approved into Decision, and Decision->DelegatedAuthority->AgentAction as the bridge between governance and AI engineering (illustrated by a Codex-PR-implementing-an-approved-decision trace Decision->CodexAction->PullRequest->Commit, provided references are preserved), with agent-run verification required to be Tool->DeterministicResult->Evidence rather than a prose 'looks good' summary. Introduces the crucial failure experiment: an agent that reads stale memory, proposes/implements/tests a change, but never checks current architecture authority produces GovernanceTrace=Broken even if technically correct, crystallized as the principle 'Technical correctness does not imply organizational correctness' via a TechnicalVerification=PASS/GovernanceConformance=FAIL experiment, formalized as two-dimensional assurance Conformance=Technical∩Governance (both a technically-valid-but-unauthorized and a fully-authorized-but-technically-incorrect implementation each yield overall FAIL), and the KnowledgeOS assurance model Assurance=Evidence+Verification+Authority+Traceability explicitly rather than Assurance=TestResult. Defines traceability completeness T=verified-links/required-links with the CriticalPath (Authority->Decision->Action->Verification->Evidence, the minimal governance-assurance path) assessed separately since a single missing critical edge invalidates the trace even at high overall completeness, illustrated by a CriticalPath=Broken experiment (all implementation artifacts exist but no authority can be established). Adds temporal reconstruction (t_intent through t_observation with consistency checks, illustrated by a verification-timestamp-preceding-implementation-timestamp anomaly) and version reconstruction (DecisionVersion->ImplementationVersion, e.g. Decision D42->Commit c81->Artifact v2.4, illustrated by an OBS-classified commit-implements-a-superseded-decision governance mismatch). Covers the multi-state reconciliation problem (DeclaredState/ImplementationState/DeploymentState/RuntimeState/KnowledgeState as potentially divergent realities that KnowledgeOS must reconcile) via the reconciliation chain Declared->Implemented->Deployed->Observed->Verified->AuthoritativeKnowledge with every transition requiring evidence, demonstrated by a strong-conformance PostgreSQL experiment versus an ArchitectureDrift experiment (declared/implemented PostgreSQL but runtime MySQL). Reiterates Detection≠Finding (a rule must interpret Expected≠Observed before a Finding is generated, illustrated by a strong ArchitectureDriftFinding record with rule/observed/expected/evidence fields) and the finding lifecycle Open->Investigating->Remediating->Verified->Closed with a lifecycle-integrity-violation experiment for closure without verification evidence. Closes with the complete target-architecture cycle diagram (Intent->Decision->Authority->Engineering Action->Implementation->Deterministic Verification->Runtime->Observation->Evidence->Knowledge Update->future Intent) and the decisive architectural distinction that a repository/knowledge base stores State while an operating system manages State+Transitions+Control+Feedback, formalized as KnowledgeOS=Knowledge+StateTransitions+Governance+Evidence+Feedback, explicitly a much stronger definition than 'AI knowledge platform.' A Step 117 verdict DEFINED (not yet PASS/FAIL, since the actual verdict must remain evidence-dependent) states the strongest test (can one real change be traversed from intent to authoritative post-change knowledge) and previews Step 118 (Governance-to-Engineering Closure Test, the reverse direction: Runtime->Observation->Finding->Governance->Decision->Remediation->Verification, the transition from a traceability system to a genuine closed-loop engineering control system).
contribution_assessment: Precedes and is directly extended by the reverse-direction closure model (S1016/Step 118), and itself operationalizes the target semantic graph (S1015/Step 115) into the first concrete forward-direction end-to-end test. Contributes the canonical EC=(Intent,Decision,Authority,Change,Verification,Runtime,Evidence,Knowledge) reconstruction structure -- explicitly not a new domain entity, a methodological device for tracing one real historical change -- and works through all eight stages with a sustained, concrete Nexus-upgrade example that gives every abstract distinction from Steps 108-116 a fully worked instance: ChangeOccurred≠WhyChangeWasRequired for Intent; Document≠Decision for Decision; Actor≠Authority plus a newly explicit AuthorityScope check (an Architecture Board's authority over architecture does not automatically extend to production operations) for Authority; strong-vs-weak ImplementationTrace based on explicit cross-referencing for Implementation; the four-way Functional/Architecture/Security/Operational verification-dimension separation (no single test represents all four) directly extending Step 108's deterministic-assurance hierarchy for Verification; a concrete DRIFT finding (build artifact v2 vs runtime v1) for Runtime, directly instantiating Step 107's drift model; Observation≠Conclusion and Observation-supports->Claim for Observation; and a concrete Knowledge-synchronization-gap (RuntimeState≠KnowledgeState) for the final Knowledge stage. summary: Step 119 tests whether the actual KnowledgeOS/EKS ecosystem closes the loop in practice, via the target Expected->Observed->Detected->Classified->Governed->Remediated->Verified->Recorded, shifting the reconstruction from 'what could KnowledgeOS mean' to 'what does KnowledgeOS actually do when engineering reality diverges from governed knowledge.' States the control-loop hypothesis KnowledgeOS=ReferenceState+Observation+Comparison+Governance+Action+Verification+Learning with the essential operation Compare(Expected,Observed) followed by controlled response. Covers reference state (nine possible authoritative sources) with a Reference-missing verdict when no authoritative source can be identified for a checker's 'differs from expected state' report, a reference hierarchy (EnterprisePolicy/ArchitectureDecision/DomainRule/ImplementationRule/RuntimeExpectation) that may conflict requiring precedence semantics, an AMBIGUOUS-verdict conflicting-references experiment (architecture requires PostgreSQL, team documentation allows MySQL, called a semantic problem not a search problem), and expected-state provenance ExpectedState->Source->Authority->Validity (illustrated by an unapproved Markdown architecture document yielding Authority=Unknown). Covers observation from ten possible sources requiring identity and timestamp, with a PARTIAL-graded experiment (a scanner result with no timestamp/environment). Defines the central Compare(R_t,O_t) operation required to be deterministic wherever possible (illustrated by ExpectedDependency=false/ObservedDependency=true->Violation=True), contrasted with human visual diagram comparison (classified Human verification, not Deterministic control) and a NON-DETERMINISTIC-classified experiment where identical inputs yield different compliance results depending on which agent evaluates them. Reinforces Difference->Classification (ExpectedChange/ApprovedException/TemporaryDrift/Violation/Unknown, illustrated by an approved-emergency-exception experiment showing Difference≠Violation) and Classification->GovernancePath routing, with a PARTIAL-graded generic-issue-queue experiment showing weak governance semantics when everything is routed identically. Covers Finding->Decision (Remediate/AcceptRisk/GrantException/ChangeRule/RejectFinding) with a weak-governance-decision-semantics experiment (a finding merely marked 'Resolved' by a human click with no decision record), Decision->RemediationAction requiring retained DecisionID (a PARTIAL-graded weak-traceability experiment where an engineer's fix commit has no finding/decision reference), and agent remediation requiring AgentIdentity+DelegatedAuthority (a PARTIAL-graded experiment where Git identifies the human account but not which agent/session performed the action). Reinforces rule-targeted verification (an INVALID-CLOSURE-classified experiment: an unauthorized-dependency finding remediated only by a code-formatting change and 'verified' merely by unrelated passing unit tests) and the closure condition FindingClosed⇒VerificationAddressesFinding (potentially also ⇒ObservedState-conforms), with a PASS-classified experiment where a closed finding is reopened after a new observation still shows the violation. Introduces the crucial three-way drift taxonomy Implementation drift (Code≠Architecture), Runtime drift (Runtime≠Deployment), Knowledge drift (Knowledge≠Reality) that KnowledgeOS potentially needs to detect all three of, illustrated by a KNOWLEDGE-DRIFT-classified experiment (correct code and runtime but stale documentation) and the RuntimeEvidence->KnowledgeUpdateCandidate principle that should not automatically overwrite authoritative knowledge. States the important ObservedTruth≠AuthoritativeKnowledge boundary (a runtime observation tells us what happened, not what the organization has decided should happen) illustrated by an agent proposing to update architecture docs to match an observed database-engine change without first checking whether the change was authorized, formalized as Observation->KnowledgeChangeProposal rather than Observation->AutomaticAuthority (preserving governance), with a risk-based human-in-the-loop boundary (low-risk derived metadata like last_seen timestamps may auto-update; architecture-authority changes like 'production architecture is now officially changed' should not be auto-generated). Refines the maturity model into seven control-loop levels C0 Observe through C6 Learn (Runtime->Observation->Difference->Finding->Decision->Action->Verification->Knowledge), stating a complete KnowledgeOS control loop requires C0+C1+...+C6 evaluated level by level rather than one vague maturity label, and control-loop integrity as only as strong as its weakest critical transition (illustrated by two contrasting experiments: excellent C0-C2 with C3=0 yields a mere DetectionSystem, not a ClosedLoopKnowledgeOS; conversely excellent C3 with C0=0 yields a GovernanceRepository unable to detect reality drift, not a closed engineering feedback system). Introduces the two-sided architecture (Top-down Governance->Engineering via Policy->Architecture->Decision->Authorization->Implementation->Deployment; Bottom-up Engineering->Governance via Runtime->Observation->Verification->Finding->Governance->Decision; KnowledgeOS positioned at their bidirectional intersection Governance<->KnowledgeOS<->Engineering) and situates agents in the middle as Participant in the Knowledge Loop (consuming GovernedKnowledge, producing Recommendations, possibly executing AuthorizedActions, generating Observations and Evidence) explicitly not the owner of organizational truth, illustrated by a PASS-classified agent-finding-candidate-validated-by-governance experiment and agent-as-evidence-producer requiring Agent->Tool->Result->Evidence with identified agent/session/tool/input/output/timestamp (a PASS-classified experiment where an unbacked 'I checked the repository' claim is Evidence=Weak). Formulates three central agent-boundary distinctions -- AgentAssertion≠Evidence (unless evidence provenance exists), AgentRecommendation≠Decision, AgentCapability≠Authority -- called central to the AI engineering platform, the LLMReasoning-vs-DeterministicAssurance separation (illustrated by a PASS-classified experiment where an LLM's 'architecture is compliant' cannot override a deterministic checker's FAIL), an evidence-priority hierarchy DeterministicVerifiedEvidence>ToolObservedEvidence>HumanAssertion>AgentAssertion>Inference (an epistemic-status distinction, not a value judgment on human evidence), and a six-value epistemic status vocabulary (Observed/Verified/Asserted/Inferred/Proposed/Authoritative) with a PASS-classified experiment preventing an agent's inference from silently becoming Authoritative -- crystallized as the principle 'KnowledgeOS must preserve epistemic status,' explicitly called one of the most important architectural properties discovered in the reconstruction. Defines closed-loop learning as requiring Evidence->CandidateKnowledge->Validation->AuthoritativeKnowledge (not a direct Evidence->Knowledge jump, illustrated by a transient-runtime-event-should-not-automatically-become-an-architecture-rule experiment) and a five-stage knowledge promotion pipeline Raw->Observed->Supported->Validated->Authoritative, with the final Validated->Authoritative transition requiring explicit Promotion->Authority (illustrated by a governance-violation experiment where an agent automatically declares a recurring pattern a 'new enterprise architecture standard' without delegated authority to do so). States the strongest invariant set so far -- No authoritative knowledge change without valid authority; No governance closure without verification evidence; No evidence claim without provenance -- together forming a semantic assurance constitution, and a candidate seven-principle KnowledgeOS Constitution K1-K7 (K1 Provenance: KnowledgeObject->Provenance; K2 Authority: AuthoritativeChange->Authority; K3 Verification: ClosedFinding->VerificationEvidence; K4 Temporal validity: CurrentKnowledge->Validity; K5 Epistemic separation: Inference≠Fact; K6 Agent boundary: AgentCapability≠Authority; K7 Traceability: Action->Decision/Authorization). Sharpens the KnowledgeOS definition by explicit rejection of four insufficient equivalences (KnowledgeOS≠KnowledgeGraph, ≠RAG, ≠AgentPlatform, ≠GovernanceRepository) in favor of KnowledgeOS=GovernedKnowledge+EngineeringState+Evidence+Agents+Feedback.
